findings.title: docs/17's 'recover reaped children's CPU from the parent's child-time counters' double counts every child that polling saw, and drops a long-lived child's whole lifetime into one interval
findings.evidence: docs/17-build-prompt.md:71 gives the sentence with no subtraction rule. man7 proc_pid_stat(5), re-fetched, cutime: 'Amount of time that this process's waited-for children have been scheduled in user mode' (a lifetime total). verify-2/reap_counters.out.txt: 'baseline sampler, interval 1: child cpu 0.27 s' / 'this process's cutime+cstime rose at reaping by 0.27 s' / 'CPU if the child-time increase is added as the brief says: 0.54 s for 0.27 s used'. a-linux/child_times.out.txt: 'truth, from wait4 inside the parent: 13.23 s' / 'polling plus the parent's counter: 19.85 s (+50%)' / 'less the last sighting of each child that ended: 13.22 s'. child_times_tree.out.txt: the result is exact (6.15 vs 6.15) only when each ended process's last child-time counter is subtracted as well. Limits: reap_counters 'grandchild last seen with 0.15 s own CPU; this process's child-time rose by 0.07 s (the launcher only)'; child_times, SIGCHLD ignored: '0.00 s'. ProcessCounters has no child-time field (models.py:71-84).
findings.impact: Built as written, polled spawn-heavy workloads on Linux are charged 50% more or worse, and 2x for a child that was seen until it ended. When a long-lived polled child exits, its whole lifetime of CPU lands in its parent's workload in one interval. Counters of 24,108 to 87,945 s exist on this machine. The spike reaches the live view and the trends. Orphans' time is recovered into the subreaper's workload (systemd --user), not the agent's.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:71, replace the sentence with: 'On Linux, also read each process's child time (cutime + cstime) and credit its increase to that process. Subtract, for every seen child that ended since the last tick, that child's last-seen own CPU and last-seen child time. This recovers descendants reaped inside the tree. Orphans re-parented to a subreaper are charged to the subreaper. Children of a parent that ignores SIGCHLD, and children not yet reaped, are not recovered. Never recover more than busy time less credited time in the interval.' core/models.py: add children_cpu_s: float | None to ProcessCounters now. In the P1 procfs reader (build list 05), add a test fixture with nested reaping.
findings.cost: Three sentences in docs/17 and one model field now. The subtraction, about 30 lines, belongs to the P1 /proc reader task.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/17:71, docs/05:65, sampler.py:80-87 and models.py:71-84. Wrote and ran verify-2/reap_counters.py: the unmodified PsutilProvider and Sampler credited a child 0.27 s while it was alive, then this process's cutime+cstime rose by 0.27 s at reaping, giving 0.54 s for 0.27 s used. Re-fetched man7 proc_pid_stat(5). Read the A-linux probe scripts. Their subtraction is exact, so the method works and the defect is the missing rule. R01 covers polling's blindness, not this recovery step. Merged the three leads. B's busy-time arithmetic (48.98 + 6.76 = 55.74 > 53.96) is only a bound, so I kept the direct measurements. Corrected one claim: orphans are not unrecoverable when every process's counter is read. They are recovered into the subreaper (child_times: the systemd user manager's counter rose 1.02 s), which is the wrong workload. Kept critical because following the literal instruction gives wrong numbers.

findings.title: On Linux a parent's /proc/PID/io absorbs the I/O of children it reaps, so polled workload I/O double counts every child polling saw
findings.evidence: verify-2/reap_counters.out.txt: 'child last seen: ... write_bytes 4.0 MiB' / 'this process's /proc/self/io rose at reaping by write_bytes 4.0 MiB, wchar 4.0 MiB' / 'baseline sampler, interval 1: child ... io 4.0 MiB' / 'interval 2: this process io 4.0 MiB (child gone)' / 'I/O a workload holding both is charged: 8.0 MiB for 4.0 MiB written'. a-linux/io_children.out.txt shows the same at 32 MB, and +32 MB after reaping a shell that only waited. Code: psutil_provider.py:77-78 calls io_counters (psutil reads /proc/PID/io); sampler.py:82-83 takes a plain delta; rules.py:208-209 sums it. Brief: docs/09-telemetry.md:12 lists '/proc/<pid>/io' with no caveat, and docs/17:71 has no rule.
findings.impact: On Linux, workload I/O bytes, run totals and the evidence for an I/O-bound verdict are inflated for every child seen with I/O before it exits, by up to 2x at each reaping level. The baseline does this today and the planned /proc reader would too. For children never seen, the jump is the only record of their I/O, so the counter stays useful once the seen part is subtracted.
findings.proposed_change: docs/09-telemetry.md, Disk I/O row, Linux cell: '/proc/<pid>/io, which also includes children the process has reaped'. docs/17:71, next to R1's sentence: 'The same holds for /proc/<pid>/io: when a seen child ends, subtract its last-seen I/O counters from its reaper's next increase.' Add a test with this probe's shape to the P1 procfs reader (build list 05). The baseline sampler can apply the same subtraction from batch.exited and parent_pid.
findings.cost: Two sentences now. About 25 lines plus a test in the P1 provider task.
findings.verification: Re-read psutil_provider.py:72-82, sampler.py:80-83, rules.py:204-209 and docs/09:12. Wrote and ran verify-2/reap_counters.py through the unmodified provider and sampler with a 4 MiB write, on disk-backed /tmp (ext4). It reproduced 8.0 MiB charged for 4.0 MiB written. Searched docs/ and R01-R37 for reap, children and io: nothing covers it. Windows per-process I/O counters do not include children, so this is Linux only. Kept critical because a stored number is wrong.

findings.title: The reconciliation invariant leaves System and Idle undefined, the baseline 'reconciliation' test checks only conservation, and with System taken from counters the invariant fails under polled spawn loads
findings.evidence: docs/17:98: 'attributed plus unattributed plus system plus restricted plus idle CPU time equals total capacity within 2%'. Neither docs/12 nor docs/17 defines System or Idle, and grep shows rules.py:36 SYSTEM is never assigned. tests/test_baseline.py:268-271 asserts only that the sum over workloads equals the sum over processes. verify-2/attribution_checks.out.txt: the test's check '... holds' while 'workloads 1.00 + idle 1.00 = 2.00 of capacity 4.00; the missing 2.00 has no term in the baseline'. Gates: docs/01:8, docs/15:13 and docs/17:269 require 'totals reconcile within 2%'. b-measurement/reconcile_terms.out.txt, quiet machine: busy time no process accounts for is 4.98 CPU-s = 2.04% of capacity, and System from counters is 0.34%. measure/reconcile_under_spawn.out.txt: one spawner 'missing 18.55 CPU-s = 13.7% of capacity', four spawners 'missing 71.28 CPU-s = 51.6% of capacity'. docs/10:10 accepts about 70% undercount of polled children on Windows.
findings.impact: If System is the remainder, the invariant cannot fail, and unseen child CPU appears as System beside a 'Reconciled' bar (docs/03:43). If System comes from counters, the P1 gate fails whenever polled workloads spawn children, which docs/10 accepts as normal on Windows, where no recovery exists. Either way the gate does not test what R07 intended.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17:98 and docs/12: define Idle as the per-core idle counters and System as kernel threads plus the interrupt and DPC counters. Add a sixth always-visible term, 'not seen by polling' = busy - (processes + System), shown beside polled workloads. State the check as: the six terms sum to capacity, and 'not seen' stays under a stated share on the quiet P1 fixture. Rename the baseline test as a conservation test and add a reconcile check that uses SampleBatch.cpu_busy_s and logical_cores. Show the new term in docs/03's 'Reconciled' line.
findings.cost: Four sentences in docs/17 and docs/12, one line in docs/03, one test.
findings.decision_question: Where does CPU time that polling never saw go? (a) Its own visible term, 'not seen by polling': the invariant holds and the gap is shown. (b) System: the invariant holds trivially, the gap is hidden, and System stops meaning kernel and interrupts. (c) Nowhere, and the 2% check may fail under polled spawn loads. Recommendation: (a), with R4's cgroup residual naming the unit on Linux.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/17:94-98, docs/01:8, docs/15:13, docs/17:269, tests/test_baseline.py:237-272 and rules.py. grep shows SYSTEM assigned nowhere. Wrote verify-2/attribution_checks.py: the baseline's assertion holds on a batch where half of capacity is unaccounted for. Read reconcile_terms.py: busy is the /proc/stat fields less idle and iowait, processes are credited as the sampler does, and the arithmetic is consistent. Did not re-time anything. R07's fix says 'a test enforces it', and that test is not in the baseline, so R07 does not justify a rejection. The Linux spawn figures were taken without R1's recovery, which would shrink them on Linux. On Windows, the first platform, there is no recovery, so the failure stands.

findings.title: On Linux, cgroup cpu.stat, readable in every cgroup without root, can name the unit where polling missed CPU; the brief uses cgroups only for tagged runs
findings.evidence: verify-2/linux_reads.out.txt: 'running as root: False' / 'cgroups: 235; cpu.stat readable with usage_usec: 235'. a-linux/cgroup_whole_machine.out.txt: 'machine busy, /proc/stat: 12.86 CPU-s' / 'sum of cpu.stat over the top-level cgroups: 12.81' / 'every process polled from /proc at 1 s: 5.18' / 'cpu.stat of the cgroup that held the spawner, whole run: 6.54; its children, from wait4 as they ended: 6.48'. docs/09:9 uses cpu.stat for tagged groups only, and docs/17:71 polls everything else.
findings.impact: Without it, CPU of orphans and other unseen processes on Linux has nowhere to go (R3) beyond what R1's child-time recovery restores. With it, the residual per cgroup (the cpu.stat increase less the polled deltas inside it) is exact and names the unit: a terminal-tab scope, a browser scope or a service. Orphans stay in their cgroup when re-parented, so this covers what R1 cannot.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17 Reconciliation, alongside R3's term: 'On Linux, read cpu.stat of each leaf cgroup each tick. The increase less the polled deltas of the processes in it is unseen CPU. Show it as "not seen by polling in <unit>" and charge it to the workload that owns all of that cgroup's processes, else leave it in the not-seen term, never in System.' Add this as a P1 task for providers.linux.procfs (build list 05), and measure its per-tick cost in phase 0.
findings.cost: One paragraph of brief and one provider task: about 235 small reads a tick on this machine, not timed.
findings.decision_question: Should version 1 on Linux place not-seen CPU by cgroup, which is more exact and costs one read per cgroup per tick, or only total it as R3's term? Recommendation: by cgroup, because it needs no privilege and covers orphans. Drop it if phase 0 shows the read cost breaks the budget.
findings.verification: Ran verify-2/linux_reads.py as a non-root user: cpu.stat is readable in all 235 cgroups. Did not re-time the sum comparison and relied on the lens's run. Downgraded from high to medium: this is a remedy for the gaps in R3 and R1, not a separate failure, and docs/10:10 already accepts the polled undercount. One correction: a scope can hold several workloads (a terminal tab holds both the agent and its shell), so the residual is per unit, not per workload. The proposal says so.

findings.title: On Windows the provider reads pid 0 (System Idle Process) as a process whose CPU is the machine's idle time, and that time lands in Restricted
findings.evidence: psutil_provider.py:44 maps every process_iter() entry and excludes no pid. In .venv psutil 7.2.2: _pswindows.py:636 'pids = cext.pids'; :736-737 name() returns 'System Idle Process' without opening the process; :938-948 cpu_times() falls back to _proc_info() user_time and kernel_time on a permission error; :789-811 memory falls back the same way. psutil release-7.2.2 proc_utils.c, re-fetched: 'if (pid == 0) { // otherwise we'd get NoSuchProcess return psutil_oserror_ad("automatically set for PID 0"); }'. proc_info.c, re-fetched: UserTime and KernelTime come from the SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION entry, with a pid 0 case only for create_time ('create_time = 0'). Its cmdline helpers open a handle through psutil_handle_from_pid, so cmdline is denied, restricted becomes True (psutil_provider.py:68-71), and the process goes to Restricted (rules.py:156). Microsoft Learn, 'Analyzing Processor Activity', re-fetched: 'The Idle process runs a thread on each processor... System Monitor and Task Manager both use the Idle process to calculate time when the processor is not busy. You can see processor time for the Idle process on the Processes tab in Task Manager (called the System Idle Process)'. a-windows-docs/windows_shaped_inputs.out.txt, stand-ins fed through the real provider and sampler: 'System Idle Process cpu_s 6.80 restricted True', 'sum of per-process CPU 7.84 vs busy 1.44'.
findings.impact: On an idle 8-core machine, Restricted shows about 7 cores every interval and process CPU exceeds the machine's busy time. Reconciliation (docs/17:98) fails by the idle share, and the 'how much is restricted' check (windows-priorities.md:51) is swamped. The planned bulk snapshot reads the same SystemProcessInformation entries and inherits the problem.
findings.proposed_change: psutil_provider.py snapshot(): skip pid 0 on Windows (one condition). docs/17:71, Bulk polling: 'Exclude pid 0, the Idle process, whose time is idle time. Pid 4 (System) and the Registry, MemCompression and Secure System processes belong to System.' docs/reference/windows-priorities.md item 3 and scripts/platform_check.py: check that summed per-process CPU over 5 s does not exceed machine busy time by more than 5%.
findings.cost: Two lines of code, one sentence of brief, and one platform check of about 10 lines.
findings.verification: Read the .venv psutil 7.2.2 _pswindows.py fallbacks for pids, name, cpu_times, memory, create_time and io_counters. Re-fetched psutil release-7.2.2 proc_utils.c, proc_info.c and the Microsoft page, and all quoted text is there. The leads disagreed on the bucket: cmdline needs a process handle, which pid 0 cannot get, so pid 0 is restricted and goes to Restricted (A-windows#2), not Unattributed (E-baseline#4). In 7.2.2, create_time for pid 0 is 0: the C comment says Python converts it to boot time, but _pswindows.py:910-922 does not. So the first sighting credits nothing, and every later interval credits the idle delta. Searched docs/, scripts/ and src/ for 'idle process' and 'pid 0': nothing. Status is verified from the psutil code and Microsoft's text. The exact size on a real machine still needs one Windows run.

findings.title: On Windows the per-core busy sum probably counts interrupt and DPC time twice
findings.evidence: psutil release-7.2.2 cpu.c, re-fetched: 'kernel time includes idle time on windows' / 'systemt = kernel - idle;'. InterruptTime and DpcTime are returned as separate fields and neither is subtracted. .venv _pswindows.py:272-277 returns (user, system, idle, interrupt, dpc). psutil_provider.py:115-122 computes busy = sum(fields) - idle = user + (kernel - idle) + interrupt + dpc. Microsoft 'Processor Object', re-fetched: '% DPC Time is a component of % Privileged Time because DPCs are executed in privileged mode.' That sentence is about the performance counter. No Microsoft page found says SYSTEM_PROCESSOR_PERFORMANCE_INFORMATION.KernelTime contains DpcTime and InterruptTime.
findings.impact: If confirmed, machine busy time, cores in use and a counter-based System are overstated by interrupt and DPC time. That is usually a fraction of one core, more during a driver DPC storm. In normal use it stays under the 2% reconciliation tolerance.
findings.proposed_change: docs/reference/windows-priorities.md item 3: add 'over 10 s, per core, Δ(user+system+idle) equals Δwall; if so, interrupt and DPC are inside system'. If the check holds, psutil_provider._system() on Windows subtracts interrupt and dpc from the busy sum (one line), and the bulk provider does the same.
findings.cost: One checklist line now; one line of code after the check.
findings.verification: Re-fetched psutil cpu.c and the Microsoft Processor object page, and both quotes are there. Read the provider and the psutil Python code. The Microsoft sentence concerns the privileged-time counter, not the NtQuerySystemInformation field, so the finding stays suspected. Downgraded from medium to low: the evidence does not establish the double count, and its usual size, well under one core, neither breaks the 2% rule nor misleads a verdict. In a DPC storm it would make the storm look larger, not hide it. On Linux the formula is right, because iowait and guest are removed.
findings.would_confirm: On Windows: t0 = psutil.cpu_times(percpu=True); w0 = time.perf_counter(); sleep 10; read t1 and w1. If, per core, Δ(user+system+idle) ≈ w1-w0, the double count is confirmed. If Δ(user+system+idle+interrupt+dpc) ≈ w1-w0, it is refuted.

findings.title: On Linux workload memory is a sum of per-process RSS, overstating multi-process workloads, and the record has one memory field for the two units the design needs
findings.evidence: e-baseline/memory_sum.out.txt: 'chrome 17 processes: summed RSS 3115 MiB, PSS 1599, USS 1369, x1.95'; 'Web Content 3: 223 / 43 / 23, x5.14'; 'all 155 own processes: RSS 11327 MiB, PSS 6659 MiB, x1.70'. a-linux/smaps_cost.out.txt, an independent probe: 'RSS 11.36, PSS 6.80, USS 6.02' GB, and 'the 25 largest hold 87% of the proportional memory'. Code: psutil_provider.py:63 sets memory_bytes to private bytes (Windows) or RSS; rules.py:207 sums it; cli.py:101 prints it in top; models.py:82 has a single memory field. Brief: docs/17:81 and docs/06:83 'Memory for totals: USS or PSS'; docs/08:66-67 uss_top_n = 25 and uss_interval 30s; docs/14:225 states only the per-process unit.
findings.impact: On Linux, the memory column of submeter top and workload_raw.memory_bytes count shared pages once per process, 1.4x to 5x per workload. The design itself does not say what the total is for members outside the 25 largest processes. Adding a second field later changes every provider, the raw schema and every reader.
findings.proposed_change: core/models.py: split memory into memory_growth_bytes (private bytes, or RSS plus swap) and memory_total_bytes: int | None, with the time it was read. aggregate sums memory_total_bytes and marks the workload partial, with a count of members that lack it. top labels the figure. docs/06:83 and docs/08:67 state what a workload total is when USS or PSS is read only for the uss_top_n largest processes.
findings.cost: A doc sentence now. The model split touches models, provider, sampler, aggregate, the raw schema, rollup and cli: more than fifty lines with tests.
findings.decision_question: When USS or PSS is read only for the 25 largest processes, what is a workload's memory total? (a) The sum over members that have a reading, shown as partial with the count measured. (b) PSS for every readable process at the cold interval on Linux, and USS for the top N on Windows. (c) Private bytes, labelled as such. Recommendation: (a) now, and measure the cost of (b) in phase 0. smaps_cost shows the 25 largest hold 87% of PSS, at about 0.8% of a core every 30 s.
findings.verification: Re-read psutil_provider.py:63, rules.py:204-211, cli.py:94-103, models.py:71-84, docs/06:82-83, docs/14:225 and docs/17:81. memory_sum.out.txt and smaps_cost.out.txt are two independent probes, and they agree that RSS is about 1.7x PSS for this user. One change: on Windows, private bytes are not double counted, because private pages add up across processes. The wrong number is therefore Linux only. On Windows the figure is a different unit (commit) from the USS the brief names. R02 and R06 chose the units but say nothing about the summed total, so they do not cover this. Moved to plan because the change exceeds fifty lines.

findings.title: Records cannot say 'unavailable': unreadable I/O is summed as zero and labelled polled, and the Restricted bucket shows 0 bytes of I/O
findings.evidence: verify-2/attribution_checks.out.txt: 'workload docker: source=polled io_read=4096 io_write=8192 (dockerd's I/O was None)'. e-baseline/interface_cases.out.txt: 'WorkloadSample with io_read_bytes=None: refused'; 'ProcessCounters with cpu_s=None: refused'. Code: rules.py:208-209 'io_read_bytes or 0'; rules.py:216 labels every workload except Restricted POLLED; models.py:142-145 are int fields; raw.py:43-44 are NOT NULL; rollup.py:56-57 sums them. verify-2/linux_reads.out.txt: '297 restricted ... I/O missing: 297, command line missing: 0, CPU above zero: 185'. AGENTS.md:44: 'A metric the system cannot deliver is reported as unavailable, never as zero'; docs/09:5 says the same.
findings.impact: On Linux, any workload holding another user's process, such as a docker rule or a service, shows a partial I/O sum as a complete polled figure, and Restricted shows 0 B/s of I/O. Stored rows and rollups carry the zeros forward.
findings.proposed_change: models.py: make the I/O fields Optional on WorkloadSample and Bucket, and add a count of members with a field missing. aggregate: when any member's field is None, set the source to PARTIAL and fill the count. raw.py and rollup.py: nullable columns, and sums that keep None. cli prints n/a. Provider: read CPU and memory, the command line, and I/O in separate try blocks, and set restricted only when CPU or memory is unreadable. Record the change in docs/14.
findings.cost: More than fifty lines across models, aggregate, raw, rollup, cli and tests. Every later provider and reader follows the same contract.
findings.decision_question: When some members of a workload lack a field, is the workload figure (a) unavailable, or (b) the sum of the readable members plus a count of unreadable ones, labelled partial? Recommendation: (b), matching docs/17:78 'with whatever is visible'.
findings.verification: Wrote verify-2/attribution_checks.py: a rule-matched process with I/O None next to a readable one gives a polled workload holding only the readable bytes. Ran verify-2/linux_reads.py: every restricted process lacks only I/O. Re-read the cited lines. One change: the path that zeroes CPU and memory (psutil_provider.py:65-66, 104-110) is rare. On Linux, /proc/PID/stat and statm are world-readable. On Windows, psutil falls back to SystemProcessInformation for cpu_times, memory_info and io_counters (.venv _pswindows.py:789-811, 938-948, 1022-1037). That path fires only when name()/exe() or create_time is denied, which is unverified on Windows. The I/O case is verified and is the main problem. Severity rests on the wrong number; the AGENTS.md line is a standing rule, not one of the three fixed rules. Moved to plan because the change passes fifty lines once raw and rollup are included.

findings.title: An inherited workload is lost when the intermediate parent exits, and the raw process table keeps the first workload
findings.evidence: verify-2/attribution_checks.out.txt: 'while the shell lives: {20: agent, 21: agent, 22: agent}', then 'after the shell exits, reparented to pid 1: {20: agent, 22: unattributed}', and the same with the parent pid left stale. e-baseline/raw_store_cases.out.txt: the process table holds '(sh, ..., unattributed, 9.1)' while the workload_raw totals hold 'builds 9.0'. Code: rules.py:130-163 rebuilds every attribution from the current batch alone; raw.py:132-133 registers a process once per file, and raw.py:158-169 uses INSERT OR IGNORE.
findings.impact: A dev server or background job that an untagged agent started through a shell moves to Unattributed mid-run when the shell exits. On Linux the process is re-parented to a subreaper; on Windows its parent pid goes stale. Attribution fails for polled agent workloads, and per-process history disagrees with the workload totals.
findings.proposed_change: attribution/rules.py: Attributor keeps a ProcessKey→Attribution map across batches, pruned by batch.exited. An inherited attribution lasts for the life of the process. Rules are retried only when exe or cmdline changes, and an explicit rule match wins. Add a test with this probe's shape. store/raw.py: with sticky attribution the process row stays right; record any change of workload as an event.
findings.decision_question: When a process that inherited a workload execs into a program another rule matches, does it (a) keep the inherited workload, or (b) move to the rule's workload, with the change recorded? Recommendation: (b): an explicit rule wins, and inheritance is otherwise sticky.
findings.verification: Wrote verify-2/attribution_checks.py and reproduced both re-parenting cases on the unmodified Attributor. Searched docs/ for outlive, reparent, orphan and sticky: nothing. docs/17:77,94 define only the order and the parent-start check. R09 covers pid reuse and R15 covers tagged-group totals; neither covers this. Kernel-tagged runs are not affected, because group membership decides them. Only the polled path fails, so high rather than critical.

findings.title: aggregate() labels a polled sum 'kernel' for any workload in kernel_workloads, and the test asserts that label
findings.evidence: verify-2/attribution_checks.out.txt: 'source=kernel cpu_s=0.40; aggregate() has these parameters: (batch, assignment, kernel_workloads)'. rules.py:196-216: kernel_workloads changes only source(). tests/test_baseline.py:268-272 asserts source 'kernel' on a polled sum. docs/14's attribution entry: 'aggregate marks each workload as measured by the kernel, by polling, or partially'. cli.py:94 calls aggregate(batch, assignment) without kernel_workloads.
findings.impact: No current caller passes kernel_workloads, so nothing is mislabelled today. When phase 2 wires the launcher, the obvious call shows the polled undercount (R01's problem) under the 'kernel' label, which the brief uses to mark an exact figure.
findings.proposed_change: rules.py aggregate: replace kernel_workloads with a mapping from workload to the group's own totals (CPU, I/O, processes). Use those totals for KERNEL workloads and keep the polled sum only as a cross-check. tests/test_baseline.py:268-272: assert the group's figure. A smaller alternative: docs/14 says the parameter is a label only and that phase 2 must replace it.
findings.cost: About 15 lines and one test change.
findings.verification: Ran the probe and grepped for callers: only the test passes kernel_workloads. Downgraded from high to medium: this is a latent trap in an API that will mislead once it is wired, not a wrong number today.

findings.title: include_children is used by the sample rules but defined nowhere, and the code ORs it with inherit_from_parent, so a rule cannot turn inheritance off
findings.evidence: docs/08-configuration.md:232,238,244 set include_children = true, and grep finds no document that defines it. rules.py:62 defaults it to False; rules.py:181 has 'inheritable=self._inherit or rule.include_children'. verify-2/attribution_checks.out.txt: 'include_children=False, inherit_from_parent=True: child cc -> builds'; 'include_children=True, inherit_from_parent=False: child cc -> builds'. docs/08:101: 'inherit_from_parent | true | Turn off to see helper processes on their own'.
findings.impact: A rule cannot decline children while the global default is on. Turning the global setting off, as docs/08:101 suggests, still leaves browser, IDE and agent children inside those workloads. CPU and memory move between workloads in ways the documented settings do not predict.
findings.proposed_change: docs/08, under 'Sample rules.toml', and the attribution entry in docs/14: 'include_children decides whether processes started by a matched process inherit its workload; a rule that omits it follows attribution.inherit_from_parent.' rules.py: include_children: bool | None = None, and inheritable = rule.include_children when it is set, otherwise self._inherit. Add one test.
findings.cost: Two sentences, about five lines of code and one test.
findings.decision_question: Should a rule's include_children override the global setting in both directions (recommended), or should include_children be removed, leaving only inherit_from_parent?
findings.verification: Ran the probe on the unmodified Attributor. Grepped docs/ for include_children and 'with children': they appear only in the sample and in the docs/02:106,116 footers. R01-R37 do not cover it.

findings.title: On Linux the baseline stores psutil's name() as exe, which differs from the executable's file name for about one in six readable processes
findings.evidence: verify-2/linux_reads.out.txt: 'exe readable: 154; name() equals the executable's file name: 130; differs: 24'. Examples: 'apport-gtk' vs 'python3.12', 'WebExtensions' vs 'thunderbird-bin', 'pipewire-pulse' vs 'pipewire'. a-linux/process_names.out.txt: 109 of 452 processes have a 15-character comm, and psutil repairs 61 of them from the command line. Code: psutil_provider.py:92 sets exe=process.name(); rules.py:78 matches the lowercased base name exactly. docs/08-configuration.md:217 calls the field the executable, and docs/14 says 'Program names match on file name'. On Windows, name() is the base name of exe() (.venv _pswindows.py:730-738), so Windows is unaffected.
findings.impact: On Linux, rules written by executable name miss processes a program has retitled, such as browser content processes, and scripts run by an interpreter. The hourly top executables (docs/17:128) are keyed by names the program can change. Attribution falls to Unattributed or to inheritance. The shipped examples/rules.toml matches only 'claude' on Linux mainly because its names are Windows .exe names, not because of name().
findings.proposed_change: docs/08, rules section: 'exe matches the executable's file name (on Linux from /proc/PID/exe where readable, else the first word of the command line); name matches the process name. Both accept glob patterns such as python3*.' Provider: store exe from the base name of psutil exe(), with name() as the fallback, and store name separately. examples/rules.toml: a comment that the names are Windows names, with their Linux equivalents.
findings.cost: A paragraph in docs/08, one model field, and two lines each in rules.py and the provider.
findings.verification: Wrote verify-2/linux_reads.py, which compares name() with readlink(/proc/PID/exe) for every process whose exe is readable: 24 of 154 differ. Read psutil's Windows name() to confirm Windows is unaffected. Changed the headline: the sample rules miss on Linux chiefly because they use Windows names; the name()/exe mismatch is the real defect. R09 concerns environment and parent rules, not this.

findings.title: On Linux the Restricted bucket holds two thirds of processes, every kernel thread among them, because restricted is set when only I/O is unreadable
findings.evidence: verify-2/linux_reads.out.txt: '451 processes, 297 restricted; all kernel threads: 160' / 'of the restricted: user process 137, kernel thread 160, I/O missing 297, command line missing 0, CPU above zero 185'. a-linux/restricted_split.out.txt: other users' processes hold 42.2% and kernel threads 3.5% of CPU time since start. Code: psutil_provider.py:79-80 sets restricted on an I/O AccessDenied; rules.py:156. Brief: docs/17:97 'System (kernel, interrupts)'. docs/10:16 says restricted processes' 'Command lines and USS are not readable', but on Linux command lines are readable (proc_readability: 134 of 134). docs/03:63 shows 'Restricted 14 processes'.
findings.impact: On Linux, Restricted reads as 'unreadable' although CPU and command line are known. It holds about 46% of CPU time since boot on this machine, and kernel threads that docs/17:97 places in System are not there. The doctor line and the 'how much is restricted' check in windows-priorities.md:51 give a misleading picture of attribution. CPU totals are correct.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17:97: 'On Linux, kernel threads (PF_KTHREAD in the flags field of /proc/PID/stat) count as System.' docs/10:16: on Linux, restricted processes lack I/O and USS, and their command lines are readable. Provider: set restricted only when CPU or memory is unreadable, and report missing fields per field (R8).
findings.cost: Two sentences now. The PF_KTHREAD check, about 5 lines, goes in the P1 procfs reader.
findings.verification: Recounted with my own probe: 297 restricted, including all 160 kernel threads, all for I/O alone. Raised from low to medium: the label misleads the doctor output and the dashboard on Linux, which is what medium means here. The CPU numbers are unaffected, so not higher. This overlaps R8, where one restricted flag stands for 'I/O unreadable'. This finding keeps the kernel-thread/System part and the Linux meaning of Restricted.

findings.title: docs/03's cost sample labels System 'kernel' and Restricted 'polled', against docs/02 and the code; Restricted memory is 0.3 GB in one and n/a in the other
findings.evidence: docs/03-cli-output.md:18 'system kernel 0.24 n/a n/a n/a'; :19 'restricted polled 0.05 n/a n/a 14'. docs/02-what-it-looks-like.md:44 '| System | counters |'; :45 '| Restricted | partial | 0.16 | 0.3 GB | 14 |'. models.py:28-34 define KERNEL, POLLED, COUNTERS and PARTIAL, and rules.py:216 labels Restricted PARTIAL. docs/03:61 prints status 'opaque', which Availability (models.py:22-25) does not include (interface_cases: refused). docs/README.md:70-76 ranks the topic files together, so 02 does not override 03.
findings.impact: The accounting source is the brief's mark of how far a number can be trusted, and 'kernel' on System claims exact group accounting that no kernel group provides. A builder copying docs/03 prints the wrong labels. The memory rule for Restricted is left open: 02 sums a working set into the USS total, and 03 hides it.
findings.proposed_change: docs/03-cli-output.md:18-19: 'system counters' and 'restricted partial'. docs/06 metric catalogue: one rule for Restricted memory, for example 'workload totals are USS or PSS; where neither can be read the total is unavailable and working set is shown separately'. Align 02:45 and 03:19 to it. docs/03:61: show 'partial' with the note, or add 'opaque' to Availability in docs/14 and models.py.
findings.cost: Three lines in docs/03 and one sentence in docs/06.
findings.verification: Re-read every cited line and checked the precedence in docs/README: no rule settles 02 against 03. Searched for any statement that cost uses different labels: none. R01-R37 do not cover it.

findings.title: docs/10 and docs/17 state the polled undercount of short-lived children as Windows-only, while Linux recovery is partial
findings.evidence: docs/10-known-limits.md:10: 'Their CPU time is undercounted on Windows, by about 70%'. docs/17-build-prompt.md:221: 'Polled workloads on Windows undercount short-lived children.' docs/05-data-flow.md:65: 'On Linux part of the gap can be recovered'. docs/03:22 names no platform. verify-2/reap_counters.out.txt: 'grandchild last seen with 0.15 s own CPU; this process's child-time rose by 0.07 s (the launcher only)'. a-linux/child_times.out.txt, with SIGCHLD ignored: 'parent's counter shows 0.00 s'.
findings.impact: On Linux the dashboard and doctor would show no undercount note for polled workloads. Yet orphans, children of parents that ignore SIGCHLD, and children not yet reaped are still missed, and the baseline recovers nothing yet.
findings.proposed_change: docs/10-known-limits.md:10 and docs/17-build-prompt.md:221: 'undercounted on Windows, and on Linux for children that are orphaned, not yet reaped, or whose parent ignores SIGCHLD'. The rule in docs/17:71 itself is fixed under R1.
findings.verification: Re-read docs/05:65, 10:10, 17:71, 17:221 and 03:22. Dropped the 'optional in 05, required in 17' part: 05:65 says what is possible and 17:71 instructs doing it, which is not a contradiction under docs/README's precedence. The missing subtraction rule is R1's finding and is merged there. My orphan case confirms the remaining Linux undercount.
